text: Every data scientist has shipped a number that turned out to be wrong. Usually it wasn't a dramatic crash — a join quietly duplicated rows, a filter dropped the wrong category, or a small tweak to a cleaning function changed a total nobody re-checked. Tests are how you catch those mistakes before your stakeholders do. The good news: you don't need a heavy framework or a software-engineering degree. A test is just a small function that checks one behavior and fails loudly when it's wrong.

A test has three parts: arrange some small input, act by calling your function, and assert the result is what you expect. Test that add underscore revenue multiplies quantity by price — build a tiny two-row DataFrame, call the function, and assert the revenue column comes out as 10 and 12 exactly. Test separately that it doesn't change its input — call it, then assert revenue isn't sitting in the original DataFrame's columns. Notice the names: each one states exactly what behavior is expected, so when a test fails, the name alone tells you what broke.

Save tests like these in a file called tests slash test underscore cleaning dot p-y. A test runner called pytest will discover every function whose name starts with test underscore, run it, and report which passed and which failed. Install it with pip install pytest, then just type pytest from the project folder. Running five tests like these against last lesson's module, every single one passed.

Here's exactly how a test catches a real bug. Suppose someone refactors add underscore revenue and accidentally types a plus sign instead of a multiplication sign. On the same sample rows, that produces 7 and 7 instead of the correct 10 and 12 — and the assertion fails immediately, right there in the test output. Without that test in place, the wrong revenue number would flow silently into every chart downstream, with nobody noticing until a stakeholder asks why the total looks off.

When the result is a whole table rather than one column, pandas dot testing dot assert underscore frame underscore equal compares columns, order, values, and data types all at once, and raises a detailed error describing exactly where they differ if they don't match. Build a one-row raw DataFrame and the expected cleaned output, run it through clean underscore orders, and assert the two frames are equal — this one test now exercises the entire pipeline in a single assertion.

There's an important difference between testing your code and checking your data. A test uses small, made-up input that you fully control, to prove your function behaves correctly. A data check examines the real data every single time it arrives — after cleaning the actual file, assert the order id column is unique, and assert every revenue value is zero or greater. Both matter, and they lean on nearly identical tools. In production, a failing data check stops the pipeline before bad numbers ever get a chance to spread.

You can't test everything, so prioritize. Business rules first — revenue, discounts, status logic — because wrong numbers here cost the most. Edge cases next — empty input, missing values, duplicates; we actually checked that standardize underscore region leaves a missing region missing rather than crashing outright. And bugs you've already fixed — add a test the moment you fix one, so it can never quietly come back.

To recap: a test arranges input, acts, and asserts, with a name that states the expected behavior. Plain assert, plus pandas dot testing dot assert underscore frame underscore equal, covers most data-code tests. Tests protect your functions; data checks protect against bad incoming data. Start with business rules, edge cases, and past bugs. Next up: reproducibility, making sure your results come out the same every time.
